title: Krishna Fights Varuna for the Celestial Cows
story:
The city of Sonitpura had fallen, and with it the war that had begun when Usha, daughter of the Daitya king Vana, carried away Aniruddha, grandson of Krishna, and bound him in her father's palace with nooses of serpents. Krishna had come with Baladeva, Pradyumna and the Yadava host; the battle had been fought and finished; and Aniruddha had been freed, the serpents dropping from his body like arrows the moment Garuda's shadow fell on them. The young man had saluted his grandfather, his uncle, the great bird, and his own father, and Usha had stood shyly at his side. Narada, who had urged the match, had asked to see the bridegroom's party jest with the bride's; and so the wedding had been celebrated, with Apsaras cutting jokes and Gandharvas singing, and the kingdom of Vana had been given to Kumbhanda, who had asked only for safety. The Yadavas were ready to leave — when Kumbhanda drew Krishna aside with one last piece of knowledge.

"Vana has cows," he said, "in the keeping of Varuna, the lord of the waters. They give nectar-like milk, and a man who drinks it becomes highly powerful and invincible in battle. It is said that drinking that milk makes a man immortal."

Krishna's eyes kindled. He had come to Sonitpura to free Aniruddha, and that was done; the boy was home, wedded, whole, and the debt of the house of Vana was paid in full. But the thought of those celestial kine — fit for Satyabhama, spoken of with wonder in Dwaraka — took hold of him at once. He asked after them, and when he learned where they were kept, his mind was filled with joy and he set out on the spot, without ceremony or delay, the way he had always gone after the things that mattered. Baladeva, Krishna, Pradyumna and Aniruddha mounted Garuda's back, and the great bird rose, uprooting trees and shaking the earth as he climbed, the wind of his wings flattening the treetops of Sonitpura, until the waters of Varuna's abode lay spread beneath them, dark and vast.

The lord of the deep was not minded to surrender what had been entrusted to him. His army came out in full array, rank upon rank, the host of the waters armed and ready, drawn up to keep the kine where they were, and the battle was joined on the shore of his domain. Varuna's host was routed by the high-souled Keshava, scattered like spray before a storm, their ranks broken and their courage spent, until only Varuna himself stood against the riders, alone on the field where his power had lived.

Then the lord of the waters loosed his great weapon — the Varuna-weapon, the might of the deep itself — and the sea rose against Krishna. Wave after wave towered and crashed, and the power of that weapon came on like drowning made deliberate, an assault of water and ruin, the sky itself darkening with the lifted sea. But Krishna took up the Vaishnava weapon, and the two met in the middle of the sky. With the energy of that weapon, the water itself was ablaze: the sea burned where it stood, the Varuna-weapon was consumed in the burning, and the lord of the waters found his own element turned against him, fire standing on the face of the deep.

Varuna stood in the wreck of his domain, weaponless, his army gone, the fire of the Vaishnava weapon still dancing on the water at his feet. He had nothing left to fight with. Yet even now, in the middle of his ruin, he did not yield the cows.
reflection: It is a strange war aim — cattle, not thrones — and a fitting one for Krishna, who was raised among cows and never quite left the pasture behind. The battle turns on a single weapon outshining another, water itself set ablaze: power shown not as more of the same, but as something that reverses the order of the elements.
content_note: Depicts a battle between Krishna and Varuna with divine weapons; not graphic.
next_story_tease: But Varuna had sworn a vow to Vana, and he was not ready to break it even in defeat.
hero_scene: Krishna on Garuda above a burning sea, the Vaishnava weapon blazing in his hand, while Varuna stands in the wreck of his army and the waves themselves burn, the routed host scattering in the background.
